title: Urinary Retention
subject: Surgery
summary: Urinary retention is the sudden or chronic inability to empty the bladder, often due to obstruction, neurogenic causes or medication effects. Prompt recognition and treatment prevent renal damage and infection.

t.b: Measures bladder volume and wall thickness; a thick wall suggests chronic high‑pressure retention.
Elevated creatinine indicates renal impairment from back‑pressure.
Detects infection or haematuria that may complicate retention.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings the top causes are: benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), urethral strictures, post‑operative bladder dysfunction, anticholinergic or opioid drugs, and infections such as prostatitis or urinary tract infection.

t.b: Assesses prostate size and tenderness; enlarged, firm prostate suggests BPH or prostatitis.
Detects infection that may cause obstruction or inflammation.

sections.p: Acute retention presents with sudden, painful inability to void, a distended bladder, and possible nausea. Chronic retention may be painless, with a history of weak stream, hesitancy, or nocturia, and may develop overflow incontinence.
Investigations are guided by availability. Bedside ultrasound is essential; if unavailable, a bladder scan can be used. Basic labs include CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, and urine dipstick.

t.b: Positive nitrites or leukocytes suggest infection.
Hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia may accompany severe retention.

sections.p: Urgent red flags are severe pain, fever, haematuria, or rising creatinine. Complications include acute kidney injury, bladder rupture, and recurrent urinary tract infections.

t.b: A rise >0.3 mg/dL within 48 h indicates acute kidney injury.
Detects hydronephrosis – a sign of high‑pressure retention.

sections.p: First, relieve the bladder with catheterisation. Treat the underlying cause: for BPH use alpha‑blockers; for strictures consider dilatation; stop offending drugs. Monitor urine output, electrolytes, and renal function.

t.b: Relieves prostatic outlet obstruction; avoid in patients with severe hypotension.
Discontinue or switch to a non‑anticholinergic analgesic if opioids are used.
Treat prostatitis or UTI based on culture.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate bladder function after 48–72 h. In chronic cases, schedule repeat ultrasound and consider long‑term therapy (alpha‑blocker or 5‑alpha‑reductase inhibitor). Educate patients on avoiding anticholinergic drugs and maintaining hydration.
Urinary retention is often mistaken for overactive bladder or simple urinary frequency. Unlike overactive bladder, retention shows a high PVR and a palpable bladder.

t.b: High in retention, normal in overactive bladder.

sections.p: In patients with severe dehydration, a normal creatinine may mask early renal impairment. A negative urine culture does not exclude prostatitis if the patient is on antibiotics.

t.b: May be negative if antibiotics were given before sampling.

faq.q: What is the first step in acute urinary retention?
faq.a: Immediate catheterisation to relieve bladder pressure.

faq.q: Why is an alpha‑blocker used for BPH?
faq.a: It relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, reducing obstruction.

faq.q: Can a urinary catheter cause infection?
faq.a: Yes, long‑term catheterisation increases the risk of catheter‑associated urinary tract infection.

exam: What is the most urgent investigation in a patient with acute painful retention? — Bedside ultrasound to confirm bladder volume and rule out obstruction.
How would you differentiate acute retention from overactive bladder on history? — High post‑void residual and palpable bladder in retention; urgency without fullness in overactive bladder.
A patient on a long‑acting anticholinergic develops retention. What drug should you stop? — The anticholinergic; consider a non‑anticholinergic analgesic.
Why is a bladder scan preferred over a full ultrasound in a low‑resource setting? — It is portable, quick, and gives an accurate residual volume.
A patient with chronic retention has a creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL. What is the next step? — Assess for hydronephrosis on ultrasound and consider urgent catheterisation.
What complication is most feared if acute retention is left untreated? — Acute kidney injury from back‑pressure.
